job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight in the student house in Leeds, make tea and head to lectures or the library. I'm doing a master's in structural engineering, so mornings are bridge design and afternoons are hand calculations and a group project on a footbridge. Evenings I cook with my housemates or go to the students' union meeting. Honestly, I'm studying partly because I had no offers last summer, and I'd rather learn than sit at home refreshing job sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say it's what I expected, a lot of noise from tech companies about not much. To friends on the course I'd say the real problem is still how few graduate jobs firms advertise. Online I'd say the hype is mostly an excuse to cut training budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, because structural design gets signed off by a person who puts their name on it. But I still owe about nineteen thousand in loans, and a plateau doesn't make firms hire more graduates. My internship firm, Halden Survey, took one trainee last year and didn't replace anyone who left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and keep my weekend shifts at the climbing wall café, which pay my share of the rent. In spring I'd send about thirty applications and ask my supervisor, Mr Okafor, to read them first. I wouldn't change how I work, because my hand calculations are the part I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. Not scared, just tired. It's the same worry I had before anyone said the word AI, which is whether anyone will pay me to do what I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you trust hand calculations. Does the course ask you to use tools you're less sure about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We use a modelling package on the course, and I use it because I have to. Last month a classmate showed me an AI helper that writes the report text and I said no thanks. I'm slow to trust things I can't check line by line, and my friend Priya says that's costing me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekly train home to see my parents, about thirty a time, then the climbing wall membership. My mum, who works in a school kitchen, would send money if I asked. I hate asking since my dad's hours at the bus depot were cut last year.

say: I'd tell the union meeting it's **hype**, used to excuse cutting training budgets.
I'd tell friends the real problem is how few **graduate jobs** firms advertise.
think: I'm relieved that **structural design** still needs a person to sign it off.
Owing about **nineteen thousand** in loans worries me more than any software.
do: Finish the master's and keep the **weekend café shifts** that cover my rent share.
Send **thirty applications** in spring and ask my supervisor, Mr Okafor, to read them.
feel: I feel **flat and tired**, with the same job worry I had before anyone said AI.
S0.quote: I'm slow to trust things I can't check line by line, and my friend Priya says that's costing me time.
fieldNote: Vera's worry is **hiring**, not technology; a plateau changes little for her.
Her distrust of tools she can't check is principled but may **slow her down**.
She hates asking family for money because her father's **hours were cut**.

steps.text: Finish the structural engineering master's and keep the weekend café shifts
Send about thirty applications to engineering firms in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where firms use software as an excuse not to take on juniors. Checking drawings and writing up site reports is exactly what graduates get hired to do. I'd say it loudly at the union meeting, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the entry-level jobs go first, and mine is an entry-level job. Halden Survey's trainee spent most of the summer writing inspection summaries, and software can do that now. I'm scared the ladder just loses its bottom rungs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Halden about a second placement, even an unpaid month, to get a site reference. I'd join the graduate section of the engineers' union before I even have a job, so there's someone to ring. And I'd sit through one workshop on the checking software, with my arms folded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't feel helpless, because I can still work hard and apply widely, but I can feel the door narrowing. My housemates are already talking about moving to cities with more openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about your loans in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the loans. Nineteen thousand in loans doesn't shrink if the job doesn't come, and the repayments start the spring after I finish. My dad says family can help in a pinch, but a pinch for him is about three months of rent, not three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among your friends do you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My housemate Jonas, who's doing a computing master's. He thinks he'll be fine because he writes code, but code is the first thing named on the card. I haven't had the heart to tell him I think the same machine that threatens me threatens him sooner.

say: I'd say firms use software as an **excuse** to stop hiring juniors.
I'd say checking drawings and writing site reports is **exactly** what graduates are hired for.
think: I think **entry-level jobs** go first, and I'm applying for one.
I'm scared the career ladder **loses its bottom rungs**.
do: Ask Halden Survey for a second **placement** to get a site reference.
Join the engineers' **union** graduate section before I have a job.
Sit through one workshop on the checking software.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because the door is narrowing even though I can still work hard.
S1.quote: Nineteen thousand in loans doesn't shrink if the job doesn't come, and the repayments start the spring after I finish.
fieldNote: Vera ties AI directly to **hiring policy**, which fits her union outlook.
Her **resistance** softens only to workshops she can attend with her arms folded.
She worries about **Jonas** (a housemate) as much as herself.

steps.text: Ask Halden Survey for a second placement for a site reference
Join the graduate section of the engineers' union
Attend one workshop on the firm-approved checking software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are not ready and nobody asked us. Two years is nothing: I'd still be paying the first year of my loans. At the union I'd say government has to step in with income support before the layoffs, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it means my degree is worth very little by the time I finish it. The master's ends next summer and the jobs I trained for would be gone almost at once. Robots on building sites come later, but the design office work goes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, move back to my parents' house and take whatever paid work is going. I'd drop the hand-calculation habit and maybe even try the AI tools, though it would feel like helping the thing that's replacing me. I'd go to every protest the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep well. Every plan I made would feel like it was written on wet paper, and I'm a person who likes a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back to your parents' house mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving home means the spare room above my dad's garage and one bus an hour into town. My mum would cook for me and I'd feel eight years old again. I love them, but I'd feel like I'd failed after four years of university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to hear it from first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to hear it from government before I heard it from a company. If nobody official said anything, I think I'd stop believing anyone. I'd have no idea whether to keep paying a loan that might become impossible.

say: I'd say we are **not ready** and the government must act before layoffs.
I'd say two years is **nothing** when I'm still paying my first loans.
think: I think my degree is worth **very little** by the time I finish.
I think design-office work disappears in **2028**, years before building-site robots.
do: Move back to my parents' house to **save rent** and take any paid work.
Try the AI tools for the first time, even though it feels like **helping** them.
feel: I feel **alarmed**; every plan feels like it's written on wet paper.
S2.quote: Every plan I made would feel like it was written on wet paper, and I'm a person who likes a plan.
fieldNote: Vera expects her **own entry** job to vanish and says so without drama.
Her **resistance to AI** cracks under pressure, with obvious resentment.
Moving home brings **shame** as well as savings.

steps.text: Move into the room above my parents' garage to stop paying rent
Take any paid work, such as café or warehouse shifts, at once
Try an AI drafting tool for the first time
Attend every union protest about graduate jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible, if people actually do it. I'd press for retraining funded by the big firms and for proper graduate guarantees. At the union I'd ask what our branch plans to demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be about twenty-nine when the machines can do my kind of work, so my whole twenties would be a bet. If I'm a structural engineer for two or three years, that's something, but I wouldn't have a long career. I'd want to stay ahead of the people who build the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, then take the first job that gives me site experience, even at lower pay. I'd put a few hundred a month into a savings account, and I'd learn to supervise software instead of competing with it. Probably also join the political party that talks about a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steady sort. There's time to be angry and then to do something with it. It's easier than the two-year one, but I'd still check the news every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your plan differ from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly lying awake over how my parents manage. My dad's pension is small and my mum's school job isn't safe either. If I'm earning for five years, I want to put something aside for them as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust that governments would act in time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for a while, no. I don't believe politicians until they put something in law. I'd rather push on my union branch and the council than send emails to a minister.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if firms fund proper retraining.
I'd ask our union branch what it plans to **demand**.
think: I'd be about **twenty-nine** when the machines can do my work.
I want to supervise the software instead of **competing** with it.
do: Take the first job with **site experience**, even at lower pay.
Put a few hundred a month into **savings**.
Join the party pushing for a **shorter working week**.
feel: I feel **anxious but steady**; there's time to be angry and then act.
S3.quote: I'd be about twenty-nine when the machines can do my kind of work, so my whole twenties would be a bet.
fieldNote: Vera moves from **protest** to **plan** once there is time.
She is saving partly for her **parents**, not only herself.
She trusts law, not promises, which matches her **regulation-first** views.

steps.text: Take the first graduate job offering site experience, even at lower pay
Put a few hundred a month into a savings account
Join the party campaigning for a shorter working week
Learn the firm's design software well enough to supervise it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd push for apprenticeships and shorter degrees that change with the jobs. And I'd keep saying the gains should be shared through public ownership, not handed to a few firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fairly settled. I'd be thirty-four, maybe with a mortgage and a decade of experience, and I think I'd have moved into inspection or site management where a person still has to be present. The thinking part of my work will change, but I'd have time to change with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, get a chartered engineer route, and ask for site-based roles rather than the design office. I'd take the loan repayments slowly and save a bit each month. Maybe learn the AI tools in a year or two, once I'm sure they're checked by someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, not afraid. A decade is long enough to retrain once and still have a job. I'd worry about my younger cousins more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger cousins to look at what has to be done in a particular place by a particular person, like inspecting a bridge or running a site. Those are the jobs that last longest on this card. I'd also tell them to join a union as soon as they start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you embrace the tools sooner or later in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm cautious. I'd want a year of the new tools running at somebody else's firm first, with errors reported, before I ever trusted them on a bridge. If it's a decade, I can afford to be late.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we use it well.
I'd say the gains should be **shared**, not handed to a few firms.
think: I'd likely be thirty-four and moving into **site management** where people still have to be present.
I'd have time to **change with** the work.
do: Work towards **chartered** engineer status and ask for site-based roles.
Pay loans slowly and **save** a bit each month.
Try the AI tools in a year or two once **someone has checked** them.
feel: I feel **uneasy, not afraid**; a decade is long enough to retrain once.
S4.quote: I'd tell my younger cousins to look at what has to be done in a particular place by a particular person, like inspecting a bridge or running a site.
fieldNote: With a decade Vera becomes **planful** and almost optimistic.
She still wants **proof** and independent checking before trusting a tool.
Her instinct is to guide **younger relatives** toward hands-on work.

steps.text: Work towards chartered engineer status through a site-based graduate scheme
Save a small fixed amount each month after loan repayments
Try the AI design tools once other firms have tested them
Apply for site inspection and management roles instead of design office jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there's no time and my loans and my parents' money problems wouldn't wait. What would help is clear income support, a guarantee of a training place and the union behind me. I'd also want somebody official to tell people the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against technology, we just want someone responsible to sign for it. I'm not afraid of machines, I'm afraid of a firm telling me my degree is a nice hobby while the repayments carry on. Most of my anger is about who gets the benefit. I'd like to be asked again in a year.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of machines, I'm afraid of a firm telling me my degree is a nice hobby while the repayments carry on.
portrait: Vera is a **24-year-old** structural engineering master's student in Leeds, studying partly because no job offer came last summer.
She owes about **nineteen thousand** in loans, works weekend café shifts and has family who can help only a little.
Her union outlook makes her blame **firms and policy** rather than the technology itself.
She is slow to adopt AI, so her **resistance** holds in mild worlds and cracks reluctantly in the 2028 one.
With ten years she settles on **site-based** work and chartered status; with two she heads home.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because there'd be no time and the loans wouldn't wait.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support**, a guaranteed training place and a union behind her, plus honest early warning from officials.
